children: SpaceX
is facing a fresh AI-infrastructure headache after OpenAI moved to cut off its models from Cursor, the coding platform SpaceX recently acquired through a roughly
$60 billion
purchase of Anysphere. The dispute adds integration risk to one of SpaceX's biggest AI bets, although Cursor's limited reliance on OpenAI suggests the immediate financial impact may be manageable.

SpaceX operates launch, satellite-internet and increasingly AI-related businesses, generating revenue through rocket launches, Starlink connectivity and newer technology ventures. Its acquisition of Anysphere expanded that strategy into AI coding software, putting Cursor alongside other AI assets under Elon Musk's growing technology empire.
OpenAI notified SpaceX on August 28 that it intends to wind down its agreement supplying models to Cursor, proposing
November 12, 2026
, as the cutoff date.
OpenAI said it could not be confident SpaceX would comply with its terms of service and cited alleged past contract violations involving Musk-controlled companies, including X.
Musk dismissed the decision, writing that he
I couldn't care less.
He also renewed his criticism of OpenAI leadership.
The practical damage could be smaller than the rhetoric suggests. Cursor co-founder and SpaceX executive Michael Truell said OpenAI models account for only about
5% of Cursor user traffic
and that the companies remain in discussions over the issue.

That matters because SpaceX's $60 billion Anysphere acquisition effectively bet that AI software can become a much larger part of the company's growth story. Losing one model provider is unlikely to derail Cursor, but repeated disputes with outside AI suppliers could complicate that expansion.
Investor Takeaway
For SpaceX investors, the key issue is less whether Cursor loses OpenAI access and more whether SpaceX can integrate Anysphere without disrupting product adoption.
Investors should watch whether the companies reach an agreement before
November 12
, how quickly Cursor can shift users toward alternative models, and whether model availability affects customer retention or usage growth.
The relatively small
5% traffic exposure

limits near-term risk. But if the dispute escalates into broader restrictions on third-party AI partnerships, investors may begin applying a higher execution-risk discount to SpaceX's increasingly ambitious AI strategy.

title: OpenAI Shakes Up SpaceX's $60 Billion AI Bet
